lessons.title: Selecting Steel for Blades
lessons.body:
For a blade that holds an edge and survives hard use, you need steel with enough carbon to harden. In most African markets, the easiest source is an old leaf spring from a truck or car. These are usually 5160 or similar spring steel, with around 0.6% carbon. Another good option is a bastard file â they are often 1095 or W1 steel, with 0.8-1.0% carbon. Avoid mild steel (like rebar or angle iron) because it will not harden. You can test a piece: touch it to a grinding wheel. If it throws long yellow sparks with a starburst at the end, it has high carbon. If sparks are short and red, it's mild steel.

When you find a candidate steel, cut a small piece and heat it to bright orange (about 800Â°C), then quench in water. Put it in a vise and try to bend it with a hammer. If it snaps or cracks, it's hardenable. If it bends without cracking, it's likely mild steel. For consistent results, try to get a full leaf spring from a single vehicle. Clean off all rust, dirt, and paint before forging. Use a wire brush or soak in vinegar overnight.

In many African towns, scrap yards and mechanics are your best sources. Ask for 'lorry spring' or 'motor spring'. A single leaf spring can yield 5-10 knife blanks. If you can't find spring steel, buy a new piece of 1080 or 5160 from a steel supplier â but that costs more. Always keep a few known pieces for reference. Mark your steel with a paint pen so you don't mix up mild and high-carbon.

Remember: the steel's carbon content determines how hard the blade can get. Too little carbon, and the edge rolls. Too much carbon (over 1.2%), and the blade becomes brittle and hard to forge. For a beginner, 5160 or 1080 is ideal. They are forgiving in the forge and heat treat. Start with one type and learn its behavior before experimenting.

lessons.title: Forging a Simple Knife Profile
lessons.body:
Start with a piece of steel about 20 cm long, 3 cm wide, and 5 mm thick. Heat it in your forge until it's bright orange (around 900Â°C). Use tongs to hold it on the anvil. First, draw out the tang: hammer the last 5 cm to make it thinner and longer â this will go into the handle. Work from the tip of the tang back toward the blade. Keep the steel hot; if it turns dark red, put it back in the fire.

Next, form the blade. For a simple drop-point knife, hammer the tip to a point. Hold the steel at an angle and strike the edge to draw it out. You want the blade to be about 15 cm long and 2.5 cm wide at the base, tapering to a point. Use light, controlled hammer blows. Don't try to shape everything in one heat. Reheat as needed. If the steel starts to crack, stop and reheat â cold steel cracks.

After rough shaping, use a cross-peen hammer to set the bevels. The bevel is the sloping part that goes down to the cutting edge. Strike at a 45-degree angle along the edge, first on one side, then the other. Keep the center of the blade thick (about 3 mm) so it doesn't warp during heat treat. The edge should be about 1 mm thick. Check your work often by eye â you want a symmetrical profile.

Once you have a basic knife shape, use a file to clean up the profile while the steel is still annealed (soft). You can also use a belt grinder if you have one. Forge the blade as close to final shape as possible to save grinding time. A good forging leaves only 1-2 mm of material to remove. When done, let the blade cool slowly in ash or vermiculite. This is normalizing, which we'll cover next.

lessons.title: Normalizing and Annealing Blades
lessons.body:
After forging, the steel has internal stresses that can cause cracks or warps during heat treat. Normalizing relieves these stresses and refines the grain. To normalize, heat the blade to 850Â°C â just above non-magnetic (when a magnet no longer sticks). Hold it at that temperature for 2-3 minutes, then take it out and let it cool in still air. Do this three times. Each cycle makes the grain smaller and the steel more uniform. For a leaf spring, 850Â°C is a bright orange. Do not quench â just air cool.

Annealing is different: it makes the steel as soft as possible for grinding and filing. Heat the blade to 850Â°C again, then bury it in dry wood ash, lime, or vermiculite. The key is slow cooling â over several hours. In Africa, a common method is to put the blade in a metal box filled with ash, then place it in the dying fire. Leave it overnight. The next morning, the blade should be soft enough to file easily. If it's still hard, repeat the process.

You can also anneal by heating to 850Â°C and then slowly cooling in a charcoal fire that is allowed to die down. Do not use water or oil. Slow cooling lets the carbon form soft pearlite instead of hard martensite. After annealing, the blade will be grey and covered in scale. Clean it with a wire brush or sandpaper before grinding.

Why does this matter? If you skip normalizing, the blade may warp or crack during quenching. If you skip annealing, grinding takes forever and you'll burn through belts. These steps are not optional â they are the foundation of a good blade. In many African workshops, smiths normalize three times and anneal once. That's a good rule. Always test with a file: if it bites into the steel, it's annealed.

lessons.title: Grinding and Shaping the Blade
lessons.body:
With the blade annealed and soft, you can grind the final shape. If you have a belt grinder, use a 60-grit belt for rough grinding, then 120, then 220. If you don't, a file and sandpaper will work â it just takes longer. Start by refining the profile: make sure the edge is straight and the tip is centered. Use a file to remove the forging scale and smooth the curves. Work slowly and check symmetry by eye.

Next, grind the bevels. The bevel is the sloping part that leads to the cutting edge. For a beginner, a flat grind is easiest: hold the blade at a consistent angle against the belt or file. You want the bevel to go from the edge up to about half the blade's width. On a 2.5 cm wide blade, the bevel should be about 1.2 cm wide. Use a marker to draw a line down the center of the edge â this is your guide. Grind until you almost reach the line, then flip and do the other side. Keep the edge thickness about 0.5-1 mm before heat treat.

Don't overheat the blade while grinding. If it gets too hot to touch, dip it in water. Overheating can ruin the anneal and cause cracks. For a file, use slow strokes and keep the file clean with a wire brush. For a belt grinder, use fresh belts and don't push too hard. After rough grinding, move to finer grits to remove scratches. A 220-grit finish is good before heat treat.

Finally, check the edge for straightness. Hold it up to a light â you should see a thin, even line. If it's wavy, go back to the file. A little time here saves a lot of trouble later. Once the blade is ground, clean it with acetone or soap and water to remove any oil or dirt before heat treating.

lessons.title: Heat Treating a Blade
lessons.body:
Heat treating makes the blade hard and tough. You need a forge, a quench tank, and a way to measure temperature. For most simple carbon steels (5160, 1080, 1095), heat to 800-850Â°C â non-magnetic. Use a magnet: when it stops sticking, you're there. Don't overheat â if the steel sparkles, it's too hot. Hold at that temperature for 1-2 minutes to ensure even heating. If the blade is uneven, it will warp.

Quench in warm oil. Canola oil, peanut oil, or used motor oil works. Heat the oil to about 50-60Â°C â warm to the touch but not smoking. Quench the blade edge-first, then submerge completely. Move it around gently to break the vapor barrier. Hold it in the oil until it's cool enough to touch (about 10-15 seconds). For 1095, you may need a faster quench like water, but that risks cracking. For beginners, oil is safer.

After quenching, the blade is hard but brittle. You must temper it. Clean off the oil and heat the blade in an oven or over a fire to 200-220Â°C for one hour. Do this twice. This relieves stress and gives toughness. You can check tempering color: a light straw color (200Â°C) is good for knives. If you don't have an oven, put the blade in a charcoal fire and watch the colors â but this is tricky. A kitchen oven is best.

Test the blade: after tempering, a file should skate across the edge without biting. If it bites, the blade is too soft â re-harden and temper again. If it chips, it's too hard â temper at a higher temperature (230Â°C). With practice, you'll get a feel for it. Always wear safety glasses and gloves. Quenching oil can flare up, so have a lid nearby.

lessons.title: Attaching a Handle: Basic Techniques
lessons.body:
A good handle makes the knife safe and comfortable. The simplest handle is a stick tang: the tang goes into a block of wood. Start by drilling a hole through a hardwood block (like mahogany, ebony, or camel thorn) that matches the tang's width. The block should be about 12 cm long and 3 cm thick. Use a drill press or hand drill. If you don't have a drill, you can burn the hole with a heated rod â but that's messy. Fit the tang into the hole with epoxy. Make sure the blade is centered.

For a full-tang knife, you need two handle scales. Cut two pieces of wood or bone to match the tang's shape, leaving a little extra. Roughen the tang and the inside of the scales with sandpaper for better glue adhesion. Mix two-part epoxy and clamp the scales to the tang. Use C-clamps or a vise. Wipe off excess glue with acetone. Let it cure for 24 hours.

After the glue dries, shape the handle with a file, rasp, or belt grinder. Round the edges for comfort. Sand progressively from 80 to 400 grit. For a smooth finish, wet the wood and sand again to raise the grain, then sand with 600 grit. You can oil the handle with linseed oil or beeswax to protect it from moisture. In Africa, many smiths use animal fat or palm oil â but these can go rancid. Linseed is better if available.

Finally, add a bolster or guard if you want. A simple brass or steel plate between the blade and handle adds strength and looks. Drill a hole for the tang and epoxy it in place. For a stick tang, you can peen the end of the tang over a washer to lock the handle. File it smooth. Test the handle by gripping hard â it should not move. A well-attached handle will last for years.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good source of high-carbon steel for blades?
options: B) Leaf spring from a truck
quiz.explanation: Leaf springs are typically made from 5160 steel, which has enough carbon to harden.

quiz.q: What is the approximate carbon content of a bastard file?
quiz.explanation: Files are often made from 1095 or W1 steel, which have around 0.8-1.0% carbon.

quiz.q: How can you test if a piece of steel is hardenable?
options: A) Hit it with a hammer
B) Heat and quench, then try to bend it
C) Scratch it with a file
quiz.explanation: If it hardens, it will snap or crack when bent after quenching; mild steel will bend.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mild steel for blades?
options: C) It lacks enough carbon to harden
quiz.explanation: Mild steel has less than 0.3% carbon, so it cannot be hardened by heat treating.

quiz.q: What color should steel be when forging a knife profile?
quiz.explanation: Bright orange (around 900Â°C) is the ideal forging temperature for most carbon steels.

quiz.q: When drawing out the tang, you should hammer:
options: A) The middle of the blade
B) The last 5 cm of the steel
C) The tip of the blade
quiz.explanation: The tang is the part that goes into the handle, so you draw out the end to make it thinner and longer.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a cross-peen hammer in blade forging?
quiz.explanation: The cross-peen is used to strike at an angle to form the bevels of the blade.

quiz.q: How thick should the edge be before heat treating?
quiz.explanation: A thickness of 0.5-1 mm prevents warping and cracking during quenching.

quiz.q: What should you do if the steel starts to crack while forging?
quiz.explanation: Cracks occur when steel is forged too cold; reheating makes it malleable again.

quiz.q: What is normalizing?
options: A) Heating and slow cooling in ash
C) Heating and quenching in oil
quiz.explanation: Normalizing involves heating to 850Â°C and letting it cool in still air to refine grain.

quiz.q: How many times should you normalize a blade?
quiz.explanation: Three cycles are standard to relieve stress and refine grain.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of annealing?
options: B) To soften the blade for grinding
quiz.explanation: Annealing makes the steel as soft as possible by slow cooling, so it can be easily filed or ground.

quiz.q: Which material is commonly used for slow cooling during annealing?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash, lime, or vermiculite insulate the blade and allow very slow cooling.

quiz.q: What temperature is used for normalizing?
quiz.explanation: 850Â°C is just above non-magnetic and is the correct temperature for normalizing simple carbon steels.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a blade is annealed?
options: B) A file bites into it
quiz.explanation: If a file bites, the steel is soft; if it skates, it is still hard.

quiz.q: What grit belt is used for rough grinding?
quiz.explanation: 60-grit is coarse and removes material quickly for rough shaping.

quiz.q: What is a flat grind?
options: A) A bevel that is curved
B) A bevel that is a straight slope
C) A bevel that is hollow
D) A bevel that is convex
quiz.explanation: A flat grind is a straight slope from the edge to the spine, easy for beginners.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overheating the blade while grinding?
options: A) It makes the steel too hard
B) It can ruin the anneal and cause cracks
D) It makes the blade magnetic
quiz.explanation: Overheating can reverse the annealing process and introduce stress, leading to cracks.

quiz.q: What is the correct edge thickness before heat treating?
quiz.explanation: A thickness of 0.5-1 mm is thin enough for a sharp edge but thick enough to avoid warping.

quiz.q: How do you check if the blade is ready for quenching?
options: B) A magnet sticks to it
C) A magnet does not stick
quiz.explanation: Non-magnetic indicates the steel has reached the critical temperature (around 800Â°C).

quiz.q: What is the recommended quench oil temperature?
quiz.explanation: Warm oil (50-60Â°C) quenches faster than cold oil but is less likely to crack the blade than water.

quiz.q: Why temper a blade after quenching?
options: B) To make it tougher and relieve stress
C) To make it softer for grinding
quiz.explanation: Tempering reduces brittleness and relieves internal stresses from quenching.

quiz.q: What is a good tempering temperature for a knife?
quiz.explanation: 200-220Â°C gives a light straw color, which is ideal for knife edges.

quiz.q: How long should you temper a blade?
quiz.explanation: One hour is standard, and it should be done twice for best results.

quiz.q: What does it mean if a file skates across the edge after tempering?
options: A) The blade is too soft
B) The blade is properly hardened
C) The blade is too brittle
quiz.explanation: A file skating indicates the steel is harder than the file, which is desired for a knife edge.

quiz.q: What is a stick tang?
options: A) A tang that goes through the handle
B) A tang that is glued into a hole in the handle
C) A tang that is welded to the handle
D) A tang that is wrapped with cord
quiz.explanation: A stick tang is inserted into a drilled hole in a single block of handle material.

quiz.q: What is the best way to attach handle scales?
quiz.explanation: Two-part epoxy provides a strong, durable bond for handle scales.

quiz.q: Why should you roughen the tang and scales before gluing?
options: A) To make them look better
D) To make them fit tighter
quiz.explanation: A rough surface gives the epoxy more grip, creating a stronger bond.

quiz.q: What is a good finish for a wooden handle?
quiz.explanation: Linseed oil penetrates and protects the wood without going rancid like animal fats.

quiz.q: What is a bolster?
options: B) A metal plate between blade and handle
quiz.explanation: A bolster adds strength and a finished look where the blade meets the handle.
